title: ShadowBinding: Realizing Effective Microarchitectures for In-Core Secure Speculation Schemes
problem: Secure speculation schemes that mitigate Spectre-class speculative side-channel attacks (such as STT and NDA) lack rigorous RTL-level microarchitectural implementations and realistic performance/cost analysis, causing prior work to significantly underestimate their overhead. Specifically, STT's rename-stage taint computation creates an expensive single-cycle dependency chain that degrades performance on wider out-of-order cores.
motivation: As speculative side-channel attacks remain an active threat, deployment of in-core secure speculation schemes requires honest microarchitectural cost analysis; overly optimistic estimates based on simplified models prevent accurate understanding of the true performance penalty and inhibit rational security/performance trade-off decisions.
method: ShadowBinding develops concrete RTL microarchitectures for two state-of-the-art secure speculation schemes—Speculative Taint Tracking (STT) and Non-Speculative Data Access (NDA)—implemented on the RISC-V Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). For STT, a novel variant called STT-Issue is proposed that delays taint computation from the rename stage to the issue stage, breaking the expensive single-cycle rename-stage dependency chain and improving IPC, area, and timing. RTL synthesis and cycle-accurate simulation are used to measure the combined IPC and timing impact, capturing the full performance loss including clock frequency degradation.
key_novelty: STT-Issue delays taint propagation to the issue stage, eliminating the rename-stage dependency chain that limits performance for wide cores, and is the first RTL-backed evaluation revealing that combined IPC+timing overhead of in-core secure speculation exceeds 35% for high-performance cores.
contributions: First rigorous RTL microarchitectures for STT and NDA on a real RISC-V out-of-order core (BOOM)
Novel STT-Issue variant that moves taint computation to issue stage, improving IPC, timing, and area over STT-Rename
Quantification of combined IPC and timing performance loss: 35%, 27%, and 22% for STT-Rename, STT-Issue, and NDA respectively on a high-performance core
Challenge to prior research consensus that Spectre can be solved at low performance cost using in-core schemes

metrics.other: IPC impact ~20% for highest-performance core; combined IPC+timing loss: 35% (STT-Rename), 27% (STT-Issue), 22% (NDA)

limitations: Analysis is limited to a RISC-V academic core (BOOM); the authors note that if trends hold for commercial high-performance cores, overheads would be similar or worse, but this is not directly measured.
primary_theme: microarchitectural cost of in-core secure speculation
